key_concepts.summary: A boxing style describes preferred tactical solutions, not a permanent label. Users can blend styles as skill improves.
Out-boxers prefer long range, pressure fighters prefer mid-to-close range, inside fighters prefer close range, and boxer-punchers blend ranges.
A fighter may lead, pressure, counter, bait, adapt, or damage-seek; this changes training tasks.
Pressure and inside styles usually carry higher contact and fatigue load; out-boxing carries more movement volume; power styles carry more hand/wrist load.
Beginners should not be locked into a style until stance, guard, footwork, jab, defense, and simple exits are stable.
Every style has failure modes. The database should store what each style is vulnerable to and how to patch it.

tactical_rules.rule: Teach out-boxing as range control, clean scoring, and safe exits; do not frame it as running away.
Pressure fighting must cut off exits and force reactions; chasing preserves the opponent's angles.
Counterpunching drills must define the opponent trigger before adding speed or contact.
Do not assign boxer-puncher work to a beginner who cannot maintain stance, guard, and exits.
Inside work starts with position and safety, not blind trading.
Power-puncher work must include setup, miss recovery, and guard return.
Style blending is an intermediate or advanced task after base tools are reliable.
Every style session should include one patch for the user's known vulnerability.

physical_demands.quality: aerobic base, repeat power, and contact tolerance
visual processing, timing, and short explosive response
mixed speed, power, stamina, and technical flexibility
neck, trunk, shoulder, and forearm robustness
max power, hand/wrist robustness, and miss recovery

injury_or_load_risks.risk: High movement style can overload calf, Achilles, foot, or knee if volume spikes.
Pressure style can increase head and facial contact if entries are reckless.
Counter style exposes the boxer when baiting or reading late.
Trying to train all style qualities at once can increase total fatigue.
Close-range work can increase clashes, cuts, and upper-body contact load.
Power-punching emphasis raises hand, wrist, elbow, and shoulder load.

training_implications.summary: User profile can store preferred style, current style, and style-learning goal separately.
Retrieval can bias drills, tactics, and conditioning by preferred range and initiative mode.
Assessments should capture what happens when the style is denied.
A block can emphasize style exploration, style development, or opponent-specific style adaptation.
Beginners should learn broad tools before narrowing style identity.
